overview.summary: Whether the next dollar of income support should be delivered as unconditional cash paid to everyone, as cash or benefits targeted to those with need, as a guaranteed public job, or as directly provided services — and whether eligibility should carry a work or conditionality test at all.
overview.scope_covered: Universal cash vs. targeted transfers, guaranteed jobs, and direct services: pilot evidence, work effects, fiscal cost, and conditionality.
overview.scope_excluded: Minimum-wage, immigration, and general tax policy; settled historical programs; monetary-theory financing debates.
overview.why_now: A decade of guaranteed-income pilots has just reported results, AI-driven job-loss anxiety is pushing income-support redesign back onto the agenda, and some states are banning local programs even as others expand them.

stats.label: Cost of a full UBI, gross
stats.note: $1,000/month to every US adult is roughly $12k × ~260M people — $3–4 trillion a year before any tax clawback or program consolidation.
stats.detail: Estimates from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, the UBI Center, and the Penn Wharton Budget Model converge on $3–4 trillion annually, depending on whether the payment covers all adults, all residents, or is capped for working-age adults. None of these gross figures net out taxes clawed back from higher earners or savings from folding in existing programs — how much that recovers is itself contested between positions. This is a structural, population-scaled estimate rather than a fast-moving one; the underlying $3T calculation dates to 2019 but scales predictably with population and prices.
stats.source_label: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget

stats.label: Federal mandatory means-tested spending
stats.note: The federal government already spends about $1.08 trillion a year (FY2024) on mandatory means-tested programs and tax credits alone — the base any redesign builds on.
stats.detail: CBO's tally covers SNAP, Medicaid, SSI, refundable tax credits and more, excluding discretionary aid like housing vouchers. Nominal means-tested spending grew roughly 65% since 2015. It's a fraction of a full universal cash floor's cost — the core of the targeted-transfer argument — but it also reflects dozens of separately administered eligibility systems, the core of the universalist critique.

stats.label: Labor-force effect · largest US cash RCT
stats.note: The largest, most rigorous unconditional-cash trial in the US to date: $1,000/month for 3 years cut labor-force participation 2 points and hours worked ~1.3–1.4/week.
stats.detail: Funded in part by Sam Altman's OpenResearch and published as an NBER working paper in July 2024, the study gave 1,000 low-income participants in Illinois and Texas $1,000/month unconditionally for three years against a $50/month control group. The decline in work happened almost entirely on the extensive margin — people leaving work rather than cutting hours — and total income excluding the transfer fell about $1,500/year relative to control.

stats.label: Work-hours drop · 1970s NIT trials
stats.note: The original large-scale US guaranteed-income trials (Seattle/Denver, 1971–82) found work-hour reductions of 9% for husbands, 20% for wives, 25% for single mothers.
stats.detail: The Seattle/Denver Income Maintenance Experiment and its sister trials in New Jersey, Iowa/North Carolina, and Gary, Indiana remain the largest guaranteed-income experiments run in the US before the 2020s pilot wave. Reductions were concentrated in secondary earners and were larger in Denver's tighter labor market than in Seattle's looser one — a reminder that local labor-market conditions shape the size of any measured work response.

stats.label: US federal poverty line (2026)
stats.note: $15,960/year for one person, $33,000 for a family of four — the threshold nearly every existing means-tested program uses to define eligibility.
stats.detail: Set annually by HHS and effective January 2026. 12.9% of Americans lived below the broader Supplemental Poverty Measure in 2024 (Census), which nets in taxes and near-cash transfers like SNAP and the EITC — the same benefits any redesign of income support has to reckon with.

stats.label: Full-time work · Stockton pilot vs control
stats.note: $500/month, no strings, to 125 residents: full-time employment rose 12 points among recipients vs. 5 points in the control group over one year.
stats.detail: The Stockton Economic Empowerment Demonstration was privately funded and unconditional, with no work requirement. It's frequently cited against the OpenResearch and 1970s-NIT findings — though at $500/month, a smaller sample, and a single mid-size city, it's a much smaller-scale test than either.

stats.label: Days worked · Finland national trial
stats.note: 2,000 unemployed people got €560/month with no conditions; employment barely moved (+6 days/year) but self-reported wellbeing rose markedly.
stats.detail: Interpretation of the employment result is complicated by Finland's simultaneous rollout of an unrelated activation/sanctions policy for the control group in 2018, which likely pushed some control-group members into work too, narrowing the measured gap. It remains the only national-government-run basic income RCT completed to date.
stats.source_label: Kela / VATT Institute for Economic Research

stats.label: Study scale · GiveDirectly Kenya
stats.note: The world's largest, longest-running UBI trial (started 2016, 12-year arm): overall labor supply hasn't fallen — recipients shifted from wage work to self-employment.
stats.detail: Roughly 23,000 people across ~200 Kenyan villages are enrolled across lump-sum, 2-year, and 12-year payment arms. Two years in, recipients started more businesses and earned more overall, with work shifting out of agricultural wage labor into self-employment rather than disappearing. It's the strongest evidence on a long-horizon UBI, but from a very different economy than the US labor market the debate mostly centers on.

stats.label: Child poverty drop · 2021 CTC expansion
stats.note: A fully refundable, phased-out credit cut the child poverty rate 46% in a single year — the largest one-year drop on record — before it expired.
stats.detail: Child poverty (Supplemental Poverty Measure) fell from 9.7% in 2020 to 5.2% in 2021, driven mainly by the American Rescue Plan's expanded, monthly, fully refundable Child Tax Credit. It reverted to the smaller pre-2021 design in 2022, and child poverty roughly doubled the following year — cited by targeted-transfer economists as evidence a phased, refundable credit can move the poverty rate fast without a universal check.

stats.label: Federal job guarantee cost estimate
stats.note: A national job guarantee at a living wage is estimated to cost $260–354 billion a year net of savings elsewhere — under a tenth of a full UBI's price tag.
stats.detail: The Levy Economics Institute's costing nets out reduced spending on unemployment insurance, Medicaid, and the EITC as guaranteed-job workers earn more. Critics argue the estimate undercounts administrative buildout and wage-competition effects on private employers; proponents argue it's conservative because it excludes the value of the infrastructure and services the jobs would produce.

stats.label: EITC's existing scale
stats.note: The EITC — the US's actual working negative-income-tax-style program — already sends $70 billion a year to about 24 million workers and families.
stats.detail: For tax year 2024, the average credit was about $2,900. It phases in with earnings then phases out at higher income, the core NIT design principle — cited by targeted-transfer economists as proof the mechanism already works at national scale, and by critics as evidence its complexity (roughly a fifth of eligible workers don't claim it) is itself a cost of targeting.

stats.label: Benefit-cliff marginal rate · median
stats.note: Households stacking SNAP + EITC + Child Tax Credit + Medicaid face a median 42% marginal tax rate on each added dollar — and some families hit near-100% cliffs.
stats.detail: AEI modeling found a Washington, DC family with one child gets no net financial gain from a wage increase anywhere between $11,000 and $65,000 once benefit phase-outs stack; an Illinois case study found a $1,000 raise costing a family over $25,000 in childcare-subsidy eligibility. Conditionality reformers cite these cliffs as the predictable cost of targeting; universalists cite them as the case for one unconditional payment instead.

stats.label: AI exposure to automation
stats.note: Goldman Sachs estimates generative AI could automate ~25% of current US work tasks, with roughly two-thirds of jobs exposed to some degree.
stats.detail: The estimate is task-level exposure, not job elimination — most exposed jobs are partially automated rather than replaced outright, and Goldman's own analysis projects AI could raise global GDP ~7% over a decade through productivity gains that historically have also created new categories of work. How much of that exposure becomes actual displacement, and how fast, is exactly what's contested between an AI-dividend UBI and other designs.

stats.label: Guaranteed-income pilots vs. state bans
stats.note: 30+ US city/county guaranteed-income pilots have been evaluated since 2019 — even as Idaho, Iowa, and South Dakota banned local governments from running them in 2024.
stats.detail: Guaranteed-income pilots (unconditional, privately or locally funded, typically $500–1,000/month for 12–24 months) spread to dozens of cities after Stockton's SEED program launched in 2019. Republican-led legislatures in several states have since moved to bar cities and counties from funding them, arguing conditionality should be a state prerogative; supporters frame the bans as pilots being shut down before their own results are in.
stats.source_label: Stanford Basic Income Lab / CGIR Dashboard; NPR

questions.text: Does unconditional cash meaningfully reduce paid work or labor-force participation compared to targeted or conditional alternatives?
questions.why: Pilot programs are the main evidence base, but they're small, temporary, and voluntary — critics say that's exactly why they can't show what a permanent, at-scale program would do, while proponents say the pattern across pilots is too consistent to dismiss.
questions.detail: Proponents point to the pattern across geographically and demographically varied pilots (Stockton SEED, the OpenResearch/Altman-backed study, Iowa UpLift, Finland, GiveDirectly Kenya): full-time employment tends to hold roughly steady, with any hours reduction concentrated among secondary earners, caregivers, and people using the cash to buy time for job search or education rather than exiting work. Skeptics counter that pilots are structurally unsuited to answer the question that matters — recipients in a time-limited trial know the money will end, so they behave differently than they would under a permanent universal entitlement. The older negative-income-tax experiments from the 1970s ran longer and closer to program scale and found larger work reductions, particularly among second earners in a household, which critics treat as a better analog for a real UBI than a short pilot. There's also a design wrinkle: NIT economists argue their own phase-out structure creates a different, more familiar disincentive than a flat unconditional check, so 'does cash reduce work' isn't fully separable from 'how is the cash withdrawn as income rises.'

questions.text: Is a genuinely livable UBI fiscally affordable at national scale, compared to the cost of achieving the same outcomes via targeted transfers, a job guarantee, or in-kind services?
questions.why: Whether UBI is affordable turns on what 'livable' and 'universal' mean multiplied across everyone, versus paying only people who qualify or show up — proponents and skeptics are often doing different arithmetic on the same policy.
questions.detail: The affordability case for UBI rests on funding mechanisms that aren't simply new tax dollars matched one-for-one against the check size: administrative savings from retiring means-tested bureaucracies, clawback through the tax system so net cost sits far below the gross 'check times population' figure, and proposed new revenue streams like an AI/data or land dividend that scale with the automation the policy is meant to hedge against. The skeptical case is that once 'livable' is defined at a level that actually replaces a living wage, multiplying it by the entire adult population produces a fiscal number that dwarfs any existing transfer program — and that the same money reaching only people below a poverty line (NIT-style) or only people who actually take a guaranteed job delivers a comparable anti-poverty outcome at a fraction of the gross cost, since a job guarantee's cost, while also large, is bounded by enrollment rather than paid to everyone regardless of need. The dispute is less about one disputed figure than about which baseline — gross vs. net cost, per-person vs. per-participant — each side treats as the honest one.

questions.text: Should eligibility for public income support be unconditional and universal, or does legitimacy and sustainability require means-testing or a work/effort test?
questions.why: Universalists treat unconditionality itself as the point — trust and dignity over gatekeeping — while conditionality proponents treat reciprocity as what makes public spending politically sustainable; this is a clash over what welfare is for, not just what it costs.
questions.detail: The case for unconditional eligibility: universal programs avoid the stigma, complexity, and benefit cliffs of means-tested systems — where earning one more dollar can cost more in lost benefits than it gains — and a program that pays everyone tends to build a broader, cross-class political coalition that's harder to cut than one only the poor receive; universalists also frame unconditional trust as respecting recipients' judgment about their own lives rather than requiring proof of worthiness. The case for conditionality: work-requirement reformers argue a program perceived as 'something for nothing' erodes the political legitimacy that sustains public spending over time, that most voters expect safety-net support to carry a reciprocal work or effort test, and that unconditional transfers risk backlash and retrenchment precisely because they break the work-for-support norm that has historically kept welfare programs funded. This tension is currently playing out directly in the live US fight between state-level guaranteed-income bans and expansions.

questions.text: Does unconditional cash outperform in-kind services or guaranteed public jobs at improving recipients' material, health, and employment outcomes?
questions.why: Cash gives recipients maximum flexibility to solve their own problems, but critics argue flexibility can't create a childcare slot, a housing unit, or a job that doesn't exist — it can't fix a supply-constrained market or replace the structure a job provides.
questions.detail: Cash-pilot evidence reports recipients using funds for necessities, debt paydown, and stability that shows up in improved food security and mental health, and proponents argue that because needs vary person to person, a flexible check reaches more of what actually matters to each recipient than a standardized service ever could. In-kind/services defenders counter that many of the largest costs households face — childcare, housing, healthcare — are constrained by supply, not just affordability, so handing out cash into a market with too few slots or units mostly bids up prices rather than expanding access, an argument that echoes long-standing debates over housing vouchers and similar subsidies. Job-guarantee proponents make a related but distinct case: a paycheck's value isn't just its dollar amount but the structure, social connection, skill-building, and public infrastructure a real job produces, and that unemployment carries costs — isolation, lost routine — that a cash check doesn't address even at an equivalent dollar value. This is a three-way comparison rather than a single cash-vs-alternative fight, and the evidence base is thinner and more indirect than the labor-supply pilot literature.

questions.text: Would a broad, permanent cash transfer be partly captured by higher prices — especially rents in supply-constrained housing markets — rather than reaching recipients as real purchasing power?
questions.why: Pilots pay a few people while prices stay put, so gains land in full. A universal, permanent transfer adds demand against fixed supply — if rents and prices absorb it, the real benefit to recipients could be far smaller.
questions.detail: Pilot evidence is partial-equilibrium by construction: a handful of recipients spend more without moving market prices, so measured gains look like the full transfer. Whether that holds at universal scale turns on incidence. Skeptics point to research showing cash-like transfers are routinely captured by third parties — Rothstein found employers absorb a large share of the EITC, and housing subsidies are partly captured by landlords and developers where supply is inelastic. Since low-income households spend disproportionately on housing, childcare, healthcare, and education — precisely the supply-constrained sectors most prone to price pass-through — the real distributional gain could be materially smaller than the nominal payment, even if headline inflation stays muted. Proponents counter that a tax-financed UBI mostly redistributes existing money rather than printing new demand, that much spending flows to elastically-supplied goods, and that the fix for rent capture is housing supply, not abandoning cash. The disagreement is load-bearing and genuinely unresolved because no permanent, universal program exists to measure these general-equilibrium price effects directly.

questions.text: Do small, time-limited, privately funded pilots tell us anything reliable about how a permanent, universal program would actually behave?
questions.why: Every pilot pays a small group for a year or two, and recipients know it ends. A permanent, universal program would move prices, norms, and lifetime plans — the channels short pilots can't observe.
questions.detail: Almost the entire empirical case for UBI rests on pilots, and their external validity is contested. The base is thinner than it looks: of roughly 122 catalogued experiments only about 52 published outcomes, ~35 used randomized designs, and ~30 measured employment. More fundamentally, the design differs from the policy on the exact dimensions that matter. Recipients know the money is temporary, so they rationally treat it as savings/smoothing rather than a permanent income change — meaning both the reassuring null effects on work and the modest well-being gains may not transfer. Samples are small, self-selected, and often privately funded, unlike a mandatory universal population. And no pilot can capture general-equilibrium effects on prices, wages, and public finances that only economy-wide adoption produces. The strongest case for relevance is convergence: across many contexts recipients spend on essentials, work does not collapse, and stress and health improve, and newer designs (e.g. GiveDirectly's 12-year Kenya arm versus a 2-year arm) directly test duration. The strongest case against is that the flagship US study (ORUS: $1,000/month, three years) itself found effects that were modest and sometimes statistically tenuous, showing how much of the debate rides on interpreting fragile, non-generalizable evidence.

positions.name: Welfare-State Defender
positions.steelman: Markets for care, housing and health are broken — building supply beats mailing checks.
positions.description: Poverty in childcare, housing, and health care isn't a shortage of dollars in people's pockets — it's a shortage of childcare seats, housing units, and clinic appointments, rationed by geography, licensing, and provider capacity that a check can't conjure into existence. Hand someone cash for a broken market and the price just rises to meet it, or they wait on the same list anyway; build the service and everyone gets it, free at the point of use, for good. Quebec proved the point: its $5-a-day universal childcare didn't hand mothers a stipend, it built the slots, and maternal employment ended up 12 points higher by age 50 with lifetime earnings up 27% — because the barrier was supply, not income. It's also the cheaper path: UCL's costed Universal Basic Services blueprint put full expansion of shelter, transport, and information services at roughly 2.3% of GDP, versus close to 13% of GDP for a cash payment of comparable value — a tenth of the cost, delivered exactly where the need is instead of diffused across everyone equally. Fix the market, don't just subsidize its dysfunction.
positions.detail: The case descends from the postwar Beveridge/NHS tradition of universal, free-at-point-of-use provision, and was formalized as an explicit rival to cash-first UBI proposals in UCL Institute for Global Prosperity's 2017 prospectus (Portes, Reed & Percy), expanded into Anna Coote and Andrew Percy's "The Case for Universal Basic Services" (2020). Gøsta Esping-Andersen's "social investment" welfare-state research supplies the academic backbone: Nordic states that built out universal childcare and active labor-market services, rather than leaning on cash transfers, post higher female employment and less inheritance of poverty across generations than cash-heavy regimes. There's real internal debate about how far the "basic" list should extend — Coote keeps a residual means-tested cash floor for people below the poverty line rather than proposing services replace all cash outright, arguing services and an income floor are complements, not substitutes. Critics, including sympathetic economists, worry state-run provision means rationing and NHS-style waitlists instead of consumer choice; proponents counter that's a funding and governance failure, not an argument for cash, and point to Quebec's own mixed record as proof of the stakes — the same reform that raised maternal employment also showed worse child behavioral outcomes in its underfunded early rollout, which the movement reads as a case for funding services properly, not abandoning them for a check. In the U.S., care-economy organizers like Ai-jen Poo and the National Domestic Workers Alliance have pushed the same logic into the childcare and eldercare fights of the 2020s, while the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities has long resisted proposals to "cash out" food stamps and housing vouchers, on the grounds that in-kind delivery reaches the intended need — nutrition, shelter — more reliably than an equivalent cash sum would.
positions.proponents: Anna Coote, Andrew Percy, Jonathan Portes, Gøsta Esping-Andersen, Ai-jen Poo, Robert Greenstein / Center on Budget and Policy Priorities
positions.representative_name: The Case for Universal Basic Services (Coote & Percy, 2020) / UCL Institute for Global Prosperity
positions.representative_note: The movement's clearest costed blueprint — full expansion of shelter, transport and information services priced at roughly 2.3% of GDP versus roughly 13% of GDP for a comparable-value UBI.

positions.name: Work-Requirement Reformer
positions.steelman: Aid should reward work, not replace it — a check with no expectations abandons the poor
positions.description: Support tied to work is not a punishment; it is respect. Money given without expectation strands people outside the labor market and hollows out the dignity and social standing that only earned participation provides, while an unconditional entitlement forfeits the political consensus that keeps a safety net funded at all. The 1996 reform proved the point: after work requirements replaced open-ended cash aid, employment among single mothers rose from 57% in 1993 to 73% by 2000, and poverty among single women with children fell from 42% to 34% — a level never before reached. Conditionality is what makes generosity durable.
positions.detail: Our lineage runs through the 1996 Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act, which abolished Aid to Families with Dependent Children and created Temporary Assistance for Needy Families — time-limited aid contingent on work or preparation for it. Lawrence Mead gave the idea its theoretical spine: a safety net is a reciprocal social contract, not a one-way transfer, and benefits carry obligations because obligations are what reconnect the disconnected poor to mainstream life. We do not pretend the record is spotless — caseloads fell faster than deep poverty, the poorest fifth of single-mother households lost disposable income in the immediate aftermath, and the employment gains stalled after 2000. Our internal debates are real: how generous the wage subsidies and childcare supports must be to make work pay, whether time limits should bend in recessions, how to extend work expectations to non-custodial men. But the core holds against universal basic income and no-strings cash alike. Work-tested support of the kind Oren Cass and American Compass now champion keeps people attached to the labor market, preserves the taxpayer legitimacy that any redistribution depends on, and treats recipients as citizens with something to contribute rather than mouths to be quieted with a monthly deposit.
positions.proponents: Lawrence Mead, Ron Haskins, Robert Rector (Heritage Foundation), Oren Cass (American Compass), Foundation for Government Accountability
positions.representative_note: The principal academic exponent of work requirements; his paternalism-as-social-contract theory supplied the intellectual basis for the 1996 reform.

positions.name: UBI Universalist
positions.steelman: Unconditional cash trusts people over bureaucracy — and work doesn't stop.
positions.description: Every person deserves a floor under them simply for existing — not because they proved need to a caseworker or cleared an eligibility test, but because dignity and freedom shouldn't be rationed by bureaucracy. Cash, unpoliced and unconditional, respects people as the best judges of their own lives, and it doesn't stop them working: Jones and Marinescu's peer-reviewed study of four decades of Alaska's unconditional Permanent Fund dividend found no overall drop in employment. GiveDirectly's Kenya trial — the largest, longest-running basic income experiment in the world — found the same thing: recipients started more businesses and earned more, not less. As automation puts a widening share of jobs at risk, a universal dividend funded by taxing capital, land, or the compute and data behind AI is the one mechanism built to reach everyone before the next disruption hits, without first making anyone prove they're deserving.
positions.detail: The unconditional wing traces through Milton Friedman's negative-income-tax debates and Martin Luther King Jr.'s call for a guaranteed income, then sharpened into today's form via Andrew Yang's 2020 "Freedom Dividend" campaign — a proposed $1,000/month to every American adult that put UBI into mainstream U.S. politics and left polls showing roughly two-thirds of Americans favorable to some basic-income concept. Writers and researchers including Scott Santens, Karl Widerquist (co-founder of the U.S. Basic Income Guarantee Network and editor of Basic Income Studies), Guy Standing, and Rutger Bregman argue a dividend must be universal and unconditional specifically to avoid the stigma, administrative error, and clawback penalties — implicit marginal tax rates that can top 80% — that undermine means-tested alternatives. Internally, universalists disagree mainly on funding mechanism: a value-added tax (Yang), a land-value or carbon dividend, or a newer "AI dividend" that treats the compute and data behind automation as a commons to be taxed and redistributed, extending the logic Alaska has run on oil wealth since 1982. Tellingly, universalists don't lean on the widely publicized 2024 OpenResearch trial (funded by Sam Altman) — where a $1,000/month unconditional payment modestly reduced hours worked, by roughly 1 to 1.5 per week — as their central evidence; instead they point to Alaska's four-decade natural experiment and GiveDirectly's ongoing Kenya study, both of which found no net work disincentive. They read OpenResearch's result not as a refutation but as people rationally using a temporary, geographically limited pilot to buy time for job search, caregiving, or schooling — exactly the freedom the policy is meant to enable, not evidence against it.
positions.proponents: Andrew Yang, Scott Santens, Karl Widerquist, Guy Standing, Rutger Bregman, GiveDirectly
positions.representative_note: Full-time basic income advocate and writer since 2013, crowdfunded his own $1,000/month unconditional income via Patreon to demonstrate the concept; Rutger Bregman has called him "by far, the most effective basic income activist out there."

positions.name: Targeted-Transfer Economist
positions.steelman: Target the dollar where it's needed and phase it out as income rises — same poverty relief, a fraction of the cost, none of it wasted on people who don't need it.
positions.description: Every transfer dollar should do the most good it can, and a dollar sent to someone earning $150,000 does far less good than the same dollar sent to someone earning nothing — so support should phase out smoothly as income rises rather than mailing an identical check to every household regardless of need. This isn't a new idea: Milton Friedman proposed exactly this negative income tax in 1962, riding on the tax return that already measures income, with no new bureaucracy required. It already works at scale — the Earned Income Tax Credit channels roughly $70 billion a year to about 24 million workers and families and lifts about 4.4 million people out of poverty (Supplemental Poverty Measure, 2024), and a $1,000 increase in EITC benefits raises employment 7.3 percentage points while cutting after-tax poverty 9.4 points. Compare that to the alternative: a UBI generous enough to matter, say $1,000 a month for every U.S. adult, prices out near $3 trillion a year, nearly the entire federal government's annual revenue, for the same or worse poverty impact once middle- and high-income households are cut in. Spend scarce dollars on people who don't need them and you've either shrunk the benefit for people who do or blown the budget trying to keep it whole — targeting is what lets a finite budget actually hit its goal.
positions.detail: The negative income tax traces to Milton and Rose Friedman's 1962 "Capitalism and Freedom," where the pitch was as much about administrative sanity as generosity: replace the sprawling tangle of food stamps, housing subsidies, and categorical welfare offices with one clean, means-tested cash transfer run through the IRS, phased out as earned income rises. Richard Nixon's Family Assistance Plan (1969-72) and several 1970s NIT field experiments (Seattle/Denver, Gary, New Jersey) were direct descendants, and though FAP died in Congress, the phase-out logic survived and was absorbed into the Earned Income Tax Credit, expanded repeatedly since 1975 under both parties precisely because it targets working low-income households rather than spraying cash universally. The strongest contemporary academic case comes from Hilary Hoynes and Jesse Rothstein's NBER work directly costing out UBI against the existing U.S. safety net: they find a UBI generous enough to meaningfully help poor families would be so expensive that even zeroing out every existing means-tested program (food stamps, EITC, housing aid, disability, roughly half of federal social spending) would barely dent the bill, and that a flat universal payment sends disproportionately more money to childless, non-elderly, non-disabled, and middle-income households than the targeted system it would replace. Robert Moffitt's decades of research cataloguing means-tested transfer programs (collected in his NBER-sponsored "Economics of Means-Tested Transfer Programs" volumes) is the field's reference point for how phase-outs, work incentives, and program interactions actually perform in practice. The position's own internal fight is over how steep to make the phase-out: taper too fast and overlapping programs stack into punishing effective marginal tax rates near the poverty line (the "welfare cliff" problem economists on this side spend real energy trying to smooth); taper too slowly and the program balloons toward the cost — and inefficiency — of a universal check. That tension, not any dispute over whether to target at all, is where the school's real debates live.
positions.proponents: Milton Friedman, Hilary Hoynes, Jesse Rothstein, Robert Moffitt, the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC)
positions.representative_note: Proposed the negative income tax in Capitalism and Freedom (1962) as a single, means-tested cash transfer delivered through the tax code to replace fragmented categorical welfare; the case is carried forward today by economists like Hilary Hoynes and Jesse Rothstein, whose research finds a livable UBI would cost more than eliminating the entire existing means-tested safety net.

positions.name: Job-Guarantee Advocate
positions.steelman: Guarantee the job, not just the check: full employment, dignity, built infrastructure.
positions.description: A job guarantee starts from what people are owed as a matter of economic citizenship: the right to work, not just a subsistence check. Government becomes the employer of last resort, offering anyone who wants one a public job at a living wage with benefits — building childcare, eldercare, green infrastructure, and community capacity that a cash payment can't buy on its own. This isn't theoretical: Levy Institute economist Scott Fullwiler modeled a U.S. program at a net fiscal cost of roughly 0.8-2% of GDP annually, self-financing in large part because it replaces unemployment insurance, food aid, and the social costs of joblessness. Argentina's Plan Jefes put 2 million heads of household to work at its peak — 13% of the labor force — and cut indigency by a quarter, proof the model scales in a real economy, not just a spreadsheet.
positions.detail: The intellectual lineage runs through Hyman Minsky's "employer of last resort" and Keynes's insight that idle hands, not idle cash, are the deeper failure of a slack economy; Pavlina Tcherneva at the Levy Economics Institute has spent two decades turning that into an operational design — federally funded, locally administered, jobs tailored to community needs rather than a one-size public payroll. William Darity Jr. and Darrick Hamilton pushed the case into U.S. politics with research for the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities that estimated a full national guarantee at up to $750 billion a year and roughly $50,000-$60,000 per worker in wages and benefits — a number proponents don't hide from, arguing it should be weighed against the GDP lift (Fullwiler put the multiplier effect at $543 billion annually) and against what taxpayers already spend cushioning unemployment rather than curing it. That case reached Congress via Cory Booker's and Bernie Sanders' 2018 pilot-program bills, co-sponsored by Gillibrand, Merkley, Warren, and Harris, and Ro Khanna has continued pressing it. Proponents lean on international precedent for proof of concept rather than pure theory: India's NREGA guarantees up to 100 days of paid rural work to over 600 million eligible workers and has been shown to raise household earnings and even lift private-sector wages nearby by tightening local labor markets; Argentina's Jefes program, born of the 2001 crisis, is the closest real-world analogue to an emergency federal rollout. The internal debate isn't whether to do it but how: a national uniform wage versus locally negotiated pay, permanent infrastructure versus transitional bridge-to-private-sector jobs, and how tightly to tie job menus to green-transition labor needs — Tcherneva's later work increasingly frames the program as the employment arm of a Green New Deal. Proponents' sharpest rebuttal to cash-only advocates is that guaranteed income only replaces what's missing from a paycheck; it does nothing to fix an economy that structurally fails to generate enough decent jobs, and it hands the state's stabilization role to a check that can be eroded by inflation or ignored, while a job guarantee resets the *floor* on private-sector wages and conditions by giving every worker a real outside option.
positions.proponents: Pavlina Tcherneva, William Darity Jr., Darrick Hamilton, Mark Paul, Scott Fullwiler, Sen. Cory Booker, Sen. Bernie Sanders, Rep. Ro Khanna, Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, Levy Economics Institute
positions.representative_note: Levy Economics Institute economist; author of "The Case for a Job Guarantee" (2020), the field's core policy text

crux.lead: If the evidence on whether cash shrinks work still cuts both ways, is the fight over universal income really about the price tag — or about whether a floor should come with no test at all?
crux.lead_highlight: or about whether a floor should come with no test at all?
crux.subtitle: The labor-supply question is still contested, not closed; running alongside it are cost, targeting efficiency, and whether support should be unconditional by design.
crux.empirical: Apples-to-apples, national-scale comparisons of outcomes per dollar: do phased targeting (NIT/EITC-style), a federal job guarantee, or direct services deliver the same poverty, health, and employment gains as full UBI once benefit-cliff marginal rates, administrative overhead, and take-up gaps are netted out — and whether AI-driven automation displaces enough work to change that math.
crux.values: Whether income support is owed to everyone as an unconditional floor — dignity and trust over gatekeeping, no stigma, no cliff — or is better directed through need, work, or contribution, so that help concentrates where it is lacking and stays fiscally sustainable and politically legitimate.

actions.title: Fund GiveDirectly's unconditional cash transfers
actions.description: GiveDirectly runs the world's largest and longest UBI study (Kenya, 12 years, $58M+ to tens of thousands of people) on the same no-strings logic universalists want scaled everywhere; donations now route through its general Africa poverty fund, which still delivers unconditional cash and occasionally funds basic-income tests.

actions.title: Track the federal Guaranteed Income Pilot Program Act
actions.description: H.R. 5830 (Watson Coleman, D-NJ) would fund a 3-year, $495M/year federal pilot giving 10,000 people a monthly unconditional cash payment with no work test and no benefit-eligibility penalty — currently in committee.

actions.title: Read the negative-income-tax case for guaranteed income
actions.description: Niskanen Center's GI21 proposal phases cash out with income (zero by $50-70K) instead of paying everyone the same check, putting its estimated cost at $876B a year versus $1.8-3T for universal plans — the targeting-saves-money argument in full.

actions.title: See the case for a federal job guarantee
actions.description: National Jobs for All Network argues meaningful, living-wage employment should be a guaranteed right, not just a check — its Full Employment plan and legislative tracking (HR 1000) lay out how a public job offer, not cash, ends involuntary unemployment.

actions.title: Back the Child Care NOW campaign for direct public investment
actions.description: National Women's Law Center is pushing Congress for roughly $700B to build a public child-care system directly, arguing a universal mother's lifetime earnings would rise $97,000 through built infrastructure — not a cash check families must find care with themselves.

actions.title: Review the case for universal work requirements
actions.description: Foundation for Government Accountability argues welfare programs should carry a work requirement across food stamps, Medicaid, housing, and TANF alike, citing its estimate that 35 million able-bodied adults on aid aren't working and framing work as the route back to independence.

actions.title: See if your city is testing guaranteed income
actions.description: Mayors for a Guaranteed Income coordinates city- and county-level no-strings cash pilots (Stockton, Providence, Somerville, and dozens more) and a Penn-based research center consolidating results — the ground-level laboratory this whole debate draws evidence from.

actions.title: Add your view
actions.description: Think a position or steelman is missing or off? Tell us.

blocking.issue: A distinct, highly prevalent real-world position — conditional-welfare / work-requirement reformers — is referenced but never given its own steelmanned position card. The 'actions' array includes an item with `"for_position":"Conditional-welfare / work-requirement reformers"` (the FGA work-requirements link), and question 3's detail section devotes a full paragraph to 'work-requirement reformers' arguing reciprocity and political legitimacy — but the `positions` array contains only four cards (UBI universalists, NIT/targeted-transfer economists, job-guarantee proponents, welfare-state/in-kind-services defenders), none of which is this position. Their prevalence_weight values also sum to only 90 (25+25+10+30), consistent with a fifth card having been dropped. This is exactly the position most implicated by the topic's own why_now hook (Iowa/Arkansas/Idaho/South Dakota banning local guaranteed-income programs) and by the topic's explicit scope ('whether eligibility should carry a work or conditionality test at all') — yet it is the one position never allowed to speak in its own voice via a genuine steelman, while all four other positions get full description/detail/proponents/representative treatment.
blocking.fix: Add a fifth position card, e.g. 'Conditional-welfare / work-requirement reformers,' tier 1, steelmanned in its own voice (banner line ≤~90 chars, e.g. something like 'Support should come with a shot at work — that's what keeps it funded and keeps people connected to the labor market'), with real proponents (e.g. Robert Rector/Heritage Foundation, Foundation for Government Accountability, the TANF 1996 welfare-reform architects, and the state legislators behind the 2024 GI bans), citing evidence they'd actually invoke (e.g. TANF work-requirement employment studies, public-opinion polling on reciprocity). Set its prevalence_weight so all five sum to 100 (~10 given the current gap), and fix the action item's for_position to match the new card's exact name.

notes: The negative-income-tax position's steelman line ('Target the dollar where it's needed and phase it out as income rises — same poverty relief, a fraction of the cost, none of it wasted on people who don't need it.') is roughly 170 characters, well past the ~90-char 'banner line' target the other three position steelmans (all ~85-90 chars) hit — a distillation/consistency issue rather than a neutrality one, but worth tightening for parity of form.

Otherwise the four existing positions are well matched in rigor: each pairs primary evidence with internal-debate acknowledgment and a direct rebuttal to the strongest opposing evidence (universalists engage OpenResearch head-on; welfare-services defenders admit Quebec's own mixed child-outcome record), which is exactly the steelman-in-its-own-voice bar this topic is held to elsewhere.

blocking.issue: A fifth position — the conditionality / work-requirement stance — is treated throughout the draft as a live, major pole of the debate (it's named explicitly in the overview scope: 'whether eligibility should carry a work or conditionality test at all'; it gets a full paragraph of its own case in question 3's 'detail' as 'work-requirement reformers'; the crux's entire 'values' framing and lead question ('or about whether a floor should come with no test at all?') hinges on it) — yet it never receives its own steelmanned position card. Worse, the actions array has an entry with `"for_position":"Conditional-welfare / work-requirement reformers"`, a name that does not exist anywhere in the `positions` array — a dangling reference that confirms this was meant to be a real position and got dropped, not a deliberate design choice. As written, a real work-requirement proponent (e.g. the Foundation for Government Accountability figure whose own policy page is linked in that orphaned action) never gets their strongest case made in their own voice with real representative names, sources, and a punchy steelman line — they only appear secondhand, paraphrased inside another position's question detail.
blocking.fix: Either (a) add 'Conditional-welfare / work-requirement reformers' as a fifth full position with its own steelman one-liner, description, detail, proponents (e.g. Lawrence Mead, Robert Rector/Heritage, Oren Cass/American Compass, Ron Haskins, the 1996 PRWORA/TANF lineage), representative_name, and prevalence_weight — matching the depth given to the other four; or (b) if the editorial call is to keep conditionality as a cross-cutting question rather than a standalone position, retarget that orphaned action's `for_position` to an existing position (most naturally the NIT/targeted-transfer economists, who already argue in the same direction) and strike or rewrite any language elsewhere that implies conditionality is a fifth peer position.

verdicts.critic: Steelman fidelity check across the four listed positions plus a search for any position implied by the draft's own framing but never given its own steelman card.
notes: The NIT/targeted-transfer steelman line ('Target the dollar where it's needed and phase it out as income rises — same poverty relief, a fraction of the cost, none of it wasted on people who don't need it.') is substantively excellent and not strawmanned, but runs well past the ~90-char 'banner line' guideline the other three positions hit cleanly — worth tightening to one clause.

The job-guarantee position's own detail cites a $750B/yr cost from Darity/CBPP while the Basics stat block cites $260-354B/yr from the Levy Institute for what reads as the same policy — not a steelman fidelity issue, but worth a footnote or reconciling note so the two numbers in the same topic don't look contradictory.

The welfare-services position's steelman ('building supply beats mailing checks') is punchy and accurate to the position's real argument (UBS/Quebec childcare framing), and unusually for a steelman section it also honestly surfaces a counter-data-point in its own detail (Quebec's early behavioral-outcome findings) — this is good practice, not a defect, flagging only because it's the strongest section on this dimension and a useful model for the rest.

blocking.issue: The NIT/targeted-transfer position's steelman/description cites EITC scale as "roughly $70 billion a year to about 30 million working families" — but the Basics section of this same draft (correctly, citing IRS EITC Reports, accessed 2026-07-08) puts the current figure at "about 24 million workers and families." Current IRS data (tax year 2024) confirms ~24 million recipients, not 30 million; 30 million appears to be a stale figure from an earlier year. The same paragraph also says the EITC "lifts more than 6 million people out of poverty annually," but the most recent CBPP/Census figure (2024, Supplemental Poverty Measure) is about 4.4 million — 6 million was true in 2013–2015 but is roughly 36% too high for the current year.
blocking.fix: Align the position description with the Basics-section figures: change "about 30 million working families" to "about 24 million workers and families" and change "lifts more than 6 million people out of poverty annually" to the current ~4.4 million (SPM, 2024) or drop the qualifier "annually" and cite a specific year if using an older figure, so the two internal EITC citations don't contradict each other.

notes: Quebec childcare steelman claims maternal employment ended up "12 points higher by age 50" — the 27% lifetime-earnings-by-age-50 figure is a real, documented finding from the Quebec long-run childcare literature, but the specific "12 percentage points... by age 50" employment figure doesn't clearly match published numbers (documented employment effects run 7.7–8 points in the studies found, without a specific age-50 anchor for the employment metric specifically, as opposed to earnings). Likely an approximation/conflation rather than a fabrication — worth tightening to a directly sourced figure or softening to 'roughly a third smaller than the earnings effect' language.

The 'Cost of a full UBI, gross: $3-4T/yr' basics stat attributes the range to CRFB + UBI Center + Penn Wharton converging — the CRFB piece itself (fetched) lands on ~$3T via Penn Wharton's own estimate rather than an independent CRFB calculation; framing three sources as independently converging slightly overstates the corroboration, though the number itself checks out.

The EITC employment/poverty stat in the NIT-economist steelman ("$1,000 increase in EITC benefits raises employment 7.3 percentage points while cutting after-tax poverty 9.4 points") is accurately drawn from Hoynes and Patel but is specific to single mothers aged 24-48 without a college degree; presenting it without that qualifier slightly overgeneralizes, though this is a common shorthand also used by CBPP itself.

All spot-checked URLs resolved to real, live, correctly-matched pages: CRFB VAT/UBI blog, CBO publication 61472, OpenResearch/NBER employment findings page, Jones & Marinescu Alaska PFD study (AEJ:Policy 2022, peer-reviewed, confirms no net employment drop), GiveDirectly Kenya 2023 results page, Goldman Sachs global-workforce AI article, HR 5830 text and funding figures, Levy WP 902, AEI benefit-cliff report, and the 2024 state guaranteed-income bans (Idaho, Iowa, South Dakota in 2024; Arkansas 2023) — all checked out as accurately described and dated.

blocking.issue: The crux lead and subtitle assert a resolved empirical verdict on the topic's most contested factual question rather than posing it as open. Lead: "Now that cash looks unlikely to empty the workforce, is the fight... really about the price tag..." and subtitle: "The labor-supply fear has shrunk under the evidence." But Question 1 in the same draft frames this as a live, roughly even dispute — proponents citing the pilot pattern, critics countering that pilots are 'structurally unsuited to answer the question that matters' and pointing to the 1970s NIT experiments' larger 9-25% hour reductions and OpenResearch's own 2024 finding of a real (if modest) -2pt LFP / -1.3-1.4 hrs/week effect. A neutral crux cannot presuppose the answer to the question the draft itself is still treating as contested elsewhere — that's a house verdict smuggled into the framing device that's supposed to hold the tension, not resolve it.
blocking.fix: Rephrase the lead so the labor-supply question stays open rather than presupposed, e.g. drop the 'now that' causal setup and either fold it in as a third open strand or ask it as a question: something like 'Does cash quietly shrink work at the margin, or has that fear been overstated — and either way, is the real fight about the price tag, or about whether a floor should come with no test at all?' Revise the subtitle to describe the labor-supply question as disputed/narrowed rather than settled (e.g. 'How much cash dents work is still disputed; less disputed is cost, targeting efficiency, and whether support should be unconditional by design'), matching Q1's own even-handed framing.

blocking.issue: The crux's 'values' axis frames the core value disagreement as unconditional-by-design vs. 'must be earned through need, work, or effort to stay fiscally sustainable and politically legitimate' (i.e., a conditional-welfare/work-requirement position) — but no position in the 'positions' array actually represents or steelmans that camp. The only trace of it is a dangling for_position:'Conditional-welfare / work-requirement reformers' on the last policy action item (pointing at the Foundation for Government Accountability), a label that matches no entry in 'positions', plus an unattributed 'work-requirement reformers argue...' paragraph buried in Question 3's detail text. The crux promises a genuine disagreement axis that has no steelmanned voice anywhere in the draft for a reader to check it against — and work-requirement conditionality is a live, mainstream US policy position (TANF/SNAP/Medicaid work requirements), arguably more prevalent than the 'federal job-guarantee' position that does get a full steelman.
blocking.fix: Either add a fifth steelmanned 'Conditional-welfare / work-requirement reformers' position (proponents like Lawrence Mead, Robert Rector/Heritage Foundation, or the Foundation for Government Accountability referenced in the dangling action item) so the crux's values framing has a real represented voice, or rewrite the crux's values field to reflect a disagreement that the four existing positions actually stage (e.g., unconditional trust vs. the earned-income/targeting logic already built into the NIT/EITC position), and fix the orphaned for_position label in the actions array to match whichever position ends up carrying that argument.

notes: The empirical axis of the crux (targeting vs. job guarantee vs. services vs. UBI, netted for benefit-cliff/admin/take-up costs, plus the AI-automation wildcard) is a genuine, well-grounded narrowing that maps cleanly onto Q2 and Q4 — no issue there.

If finding 1's fix keeps any claim that the labor-supply fear has 'shrunk,' consider hedging with 'on balance' or similar rather than a flat declarative, since two of the five cited pilots (1970s NIT, OpenResearch) did find real work reductions.
